_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: A reflection of a reflection [bavua levavua]: a shadow of his shadow.
rashi:a1.2: And this is nothing: a person should not do this, lest it turn out to be a bad sign, and he will be distressed and his fortune will turn bad.
rashi:a2.2: Rubya: fenugreek. Some of these grow quickly, and some are sweet.
rashi:a4.2: And not on the palaces of Pumbedita: for they were robbers, as we say in the chapter HaOr VehaRotev (Ḥullin 127a): If a man of Pumbedita accompanies you, change your lodging.
rashi:a4.3: Rotten gildana: a small fish that has gone foul, as we say in the first chapter of Mo’ed Katan (11a): A fish close to its rotting is best.
rashi:a4.4: Than kutḥa that tosses rocks: even kutḥa that is excellent and strong, so that it breaks the stone when it is poured onto a stone; even so, do not eat of it, as we say in the chapter Elu Overin (Pesaḥim 42a): Three things were said about kutḥa: it dulls the heart, and so on.
rashi:a4.5: Kefei: rock, as we translate [into Aramaic] sela [rock] as kefa.
rashi:a6.1: And if he smelled it: incense of the community, he is exempt.
rashi:a7.1: Sound: one who benefits from the sound of the lyres and harps that are service vessels.
rashi:a7.2: And sight: one who benefits from the beautiful sight of the Sanctuary.
rashi:a8.1: And it answers, smell: where it says there is no misuse, that is after its column of smoke has risen, when its mitzva has been performed; and where it says he has misused, that is before then.
rashi:a9.1: The removal of the ashes: one is liable for misusing it, as it is written: “And he shall put it [vesamo],” which implies: there [sham] shall be its interment.
rashi:a13.1: There, the heifer [sham et ha’egla]: there shall be its burial forever.
rashi:a14.1: That had its neck broken [ha’arufa]: implies this one, yes; another, no.
rashi:a15.1: The balm [tzori]: the resin of nataf [stacte], as is explained below: a resin [dripping] from the ketaf trees. Resin is something that drips from a tree, and it is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a15.2: Onycha [tziporen]: sheḥelet, which we translate [into Aramaic] as tufra [nail], for it is smooth like a fingernail.
rashi:a15.3: Galbanum [ḥelbena]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a15.4: Spikenard [shibbolet nerd]: it is a single ingredient, and in the vernacular (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a15.5: Kilufa [aromatic bark]: a spice, and this is what is called kinamon.
rashi:a15.6: [Headed “nine kav” in parentheses:] The sum total is 368 maneh.
rashi:a15.7: Lye [borit]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a15.8: Karshina: brought from that place. Another version: an herb called by a vernacular name, from which they make borit, also called by a vernacular name (Rashi adds Old French glosses); so I heard from the mouth of the great teacher.
rashi:a15.9: Cyprus wine: which comes from a place called Kafras. Another explanation, in the margin: Cyprus wine is made from the kafra of a tree whose name is kafras, such as the caper bush, and the kafras [is its fruit]. [The note ends with an abbreviation, מ״ר.]
rashi:a15.11: The smoke raiser [ma’aleh ashan]: the name of an herb.
rashi:a15.12: Jordan amber [kippat hayarden]: an herb that grows on the bank of the Jordan.
rashi:a16.1: He has disqualified it: as it is written: “For any leaven and any honey” (Leviticus 2:11).
rashi:a16.2: Liable to death: when he brings it in on Yom Kippur, as it is written (Leviticus 16): “That he not come at all times into the sacred place … that he not die … With this shall Aaron come,” and so on. When he brings in incense that is not in accordance with its halakha, it is an empty entry, and he is liable to death.
rashi:a16.3: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: he comes to explain. [Rashi’s text reads Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; the Davidson English reads Rabbi Shimon.]
rashi:a16.5: So that it should be pleasant: for it is black.
rashi:a16.6: So that it should be strong: so that its scent should be strong.
rashi:a16.7: Into the Temple: for they would blend it in the Temple courtyard.
rashi:a17.1: It supports him, and so on: since it does not explain that they should soak the spices outside, at the time of soaking, and put urine on them, it supports him, who says that all its actions are in the sacred place, in the courtyard.
rashi:a18.1: One who consecrates his possessions: we maintain that unspecified consecrations are for Temple maintenance.
rashi:a18.2: And there were among them items suitable for communal offerings: for we maintain that when one consecrates his possessions and among them is an item fit for the altar, it never leaves the altar’s domain. What is fit for an individual is sold to an individual who needs an offering; what is fit for the community cannot be sacrificed [as it is], for it must be bought with the collection from the chests. Therefore they give it to the artisans as their wages. And in the Gemara it is explained as referring to the artisans of the House of Avtinas, who would take incense. [The mishna is] in tractate Shekalim, in the chapter HaTeruma, “What would they do” (4:4).
rashi:a19.1: He already taught them: there in tractate Shekalim; and those are fit for an individual as well as for the community.
rashi:a19.2: Domesticated and undomesticated animals: not precisely.
rashi:a19.3: Rather, is it not incense: which is fit only for the community? Evidently one may make incense from non-sacred materials and outside [the Temple], and this is difficult for Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina.
rashi:a20.1: To that which is given, and so on: in fact it was made in the sacred place, and they had not yet managed to buy it back from him when he consecrated it.
rashi:a20.2: The leftover incense: for every year some would remain from those three extra maneh that the High Priest brings in, since he burned only his full handfuls and the leftover remained. That leftover was not fit for the next year, from Nisan onward, for Nisan is the new year for the collection of the shekels, as the Torah said: Renew, and bring an offering from the new collection, in tractate Rosh HaShana (7a). And what would they do with it?
rashi:a20.3: They would set aside: from the Temple maintenance funds, the wages of the artisans who repair the Temple.
rashi:a20.4: And they would desacralize: this leftover onto (leftover) money; for as long as it is in its sanctity they may not give it to the artisans, since anything fit for the altar never leaves the altar’s domain.
rashi:a21.1: We do not read “Rav Yehuda teaches”; rather the text reads: With regard to all the leftovers he teaches: They return, and so on, and here he does not teach it. Since with regard to all the leftovers given to the artisans he teaches that they return and buy them back, and here he does not teach so, it follows that it is not speaking of real incense but of incense that had become non-sacred, which it calls fit for communal offerings. And this is a refutation of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina.
rashi:a22.1: Rather, Rav Yosef said: the “suitable items” it teaches means one of the ingredients of the incense, not blended incense.
rashi:a23.1: 368 maneh: for so the sum of the spices above comes out. Lye, wine and the smoke raiser are not spices.
tosafot:a7.1: Sound: this is not the sound of the Levites but kinds of music of the service vessels; and likewise the smell of the incense. And there, at any rate, there is a prohibition, as stated in Pesaḥim. But smelling wine of idolatrous libations, or a carcass, is a dispute between Abaye and Rava in Pesaḥim.
tosafot:a14.1: Two exclusions are written: this is puzzling. One exclusion would also suffice, for one could not then derive from the other, since if so, why would I need the exclusion?
tosafot:a15.1: Sodomite salt, a quarter: Rabbi Moshe Kohen explains: that is, if he has no Cyprus wine he brings in its place white wine and Sodomite salt, to soak the onycha in them; not that he mixes salt into the incense, according to the one who says the incense does not require salt. And even according to the one who says it requires salt, that is only at the time of burning, like all the offerings burned on the altar, which require salt. And Rabbi Natan’s “also Jordan amber” is likewise for soaking the onycha.
tosafot:a16.1: If he placed honey in it he has disqualified it: in the Torat Kohanim: “Honey”: I have only items for which honey is not good; from where do I include the incense, for which the blenders say honey is good? As is stated in the Yerushalmi: Had he put a little honey into it, no one in the world could withstand its scent. The verse says: “Any honey.”
tosafot:a17.1: It supports Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina: that is, since it says that it was made in the courtyard. But even if they had made it outside the courtyard, they would not soak it in urine, for it is no less than a shofar, which has no sanctity but is an accessory of a mitzva (and we maintain that such accessories are discarded), and it is taught at the end of Rosh HaShana: wine or water may be put into it to clean it, but urine is forbidden out of respect. All the more so the incense, which is burned in the innermost sanctum on Yom Kippur. Rather, it states a novelty: that even to bring it inside is forbidden out of respect, all the more so to soak it in it.
tosafot:a19.1: If a domesticated animal, an undomesticated animal or a bird, it already taught it: for it teaches domesticated animal explicitly, and in the chapter HaTeruma it concludes with “other possessions,” which means undomesticated animals and birds. [Tosafot’s heading adds “or a bird.”]
tosafot:a20.1: They would set aside from it, and so on: that is, they would set aside from the leftover; they would estimate and calculate how much that leftover would be, and desacralize it onto the money of the building artisans. In Me’ila the reason is explained, and there it is derived from a verse, as it is written: “And let them make Me a sanctuary”: let them make it for Me, from what is Mine.
gershom:a1.1: [A printer’s marker: up to here belongs to 5b.] And this is nothing: for perhaps he will not see, and even so he would return in peace; and perhaps he will become despondent and not see. And perhaps, since he is particular and becomes despondent for nothing, his fortune will turn bad.
gershom:a2.1: And rubya: fenugreek; for all these grow quickly, that is: so may his possessions grow.
gershom:a3.1: Study: learn the baraitot first, and then go up, so that you will know how to ask and to bring proof from them.
gershom:a4.1: May your learning extend for long days.
gershom:a5.1: Dwell on the garbage piles of Mata Meḥasya: that you should live there, in a place of Sages.
gershom:a6.1: And not the palaces: not in the palaces of Pumbedita, in a place of ignoramuses.
gershom:a7.1: Better to eat rotten gildana than kutḥa that tosses rocks: even though it is so sharp that when it falls on a stone the stone splits, it is better to eat rotten gildana, because kutḥa dulls the heart.
gershom:a8.1: And if he smelled it: that which he makes for the community, he is exempt, but he has misused it.
gershom:a10.1: And sight: if he feasts his eyes on the Holy of Holies.
gershom:a12.1: Its column [timrato]: its smoke. Hence before its column has risen, it is subject to misuse.
gershom:a13.1: There is the removal of the ashes, from which he would remove his full handful and place it beside the altar; this is its mitzva, and one who moves it from beside the altar is liable for misuse.
gershom:a14.1: It works out well according to the Rabbis: who say they require interment, so that one may not move them; these are two verses.
gershom:a15.1: The blending of the incense: the balm [tzori], which is nataf. And why is it called nataf? Because it drips [notef] from the ketav tree, as Rabban Shimon said: The balm is nothing but a resin from the ketav trees.
gershom:a16.1: The onycha [tziporen]: this is sheḥelet, as we translate: netofa and tarofa.
gershom:a17.1: The weight of each one is seventy maneh.
gershom:a19.1: Spikenard: in the vernacular (Rabbeinu Gershom adds a vernacular gloss).
gershom:a21.1: And the aromatic bark [kilufa]: it has not been explained to us what spice it is.
gershom:a22.1: These are excluded from the category of drugs and spices.
gershom:a23.1: Kersannah lye [borit karshina]: of that place; and some say karshina is from the fat of a year-old lamb.
gershom:a24.1: And Cyprus wine: which is made from the caper-berries of the caper bush.
gershom:a25.1: Jordan amber [kippat hayarden]: a spice that grows on the bank of the Jordan. And some say it is the excrement of a fish, and it is called ambra in the vernacular.
gershom:a26.1: If he omitted one of its spices he is liable to death: as it is written: “That he not come at all times into the sacred place,” that is, an empty entry, “before the Ark-cover that is upon the Ark, that he not die, for in the cloud”: that is, when he enters and burns it as he goes and raises a cloud, he will not die; hence if he omitted anything, he will die.
gershom:a27.1: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: he explains what tzori is. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel; the Davidson English reads Rabbi Shimon.]
gershom:a28.1: That one rubs in it: that one washes the onycha in it so that it should be pleasant.
gershom:a29.1: So that it should be strong: so that its scent should diffuse.
gershom:a30.1: For one does not bring urine into the Temple: into the courtyard, the place where it is made.
gershom:a31.1: It supports Rabbi Ḥanina [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina]: all the acts of its preparation should be only in the sacred place, in the courtyard.
gershom:a32.1: If domesticated, undomesticated animals or birds, it already taught it in that same mishna in Shekalim; and wines and oils, it also taught explicitly.
gershom:a33.1: Rather, is it not incense? And since it says “his possessions, and there was incense among them,” evidently he made that incense in a non-sacred place; for had it been made in the sacred place, it would belong to the community. Evidently its preparation may be in a non-sacred place.
gershom:a34.1: Rabbi Oshaya said: it is not speaking of communal incense, whose preparation is in the sacred place. (And what) [And why] does it call it his possessions? Because it is speaking of that which is given as wages to the artisans who do work for Temple maintenance.
gershom:a35.1: As it is taught: The leftover incense: that is, what remains of those three extra maneh after he took his full handfuls from them on Yom Kippur, as it says below.
gershom:a36.1: What would they do with it? They would set aside from it the artisans’ wages and desacralize it onto the artisans’ money. For so Shmuel said in tractate Me’ila (14a): One builds with non-sacred materials and afterward consecrates. That is, the artisans would buy the building materials with their own money and build, and when it was built, the treasurers would take consecrated money equal to what the artisans had laid out and transfer its sanctity onto the building; the building became consecrated and the consecrated money went out to non-sacred status. Afterward they would bring leftover incense equal to that money, the artisans’ fee, and desacralize the incense onto that money that had been consecrated; the money returned to its sanctity, and the incense went out to non-sacred status.
gershom:a37.1: And they give it to the artisans as their wages: those coins they would give to the House of Garmu and the House of Avtinas as their wages. Then they would buy that incense back from the artisans with the new collection, from the money of the chamber, and mix it with the new incense, and it is all new, since it was bought with the new collection. And if the artisan consecrated his possessions while the incense was in his hand, the mishna speaks of that incense, whose preparation was in the sacred place, and there is no difficulty.
gershom:a38.1: Rav Yosef objects to this: can you say that it is speaking of that? But with regard to all the leftovers of offerings, whether wine or animals, Rav Yehuda teaches: They buy them back from the artisans with the new collection, and they were fit for offerings. And here, with one who consecrates his possessions, which we established as referring to incense, it does not teach that they buy it back with the new collection; it teaches only that they are given to the artisans as their wages, and not that they buy it back. Since it does not teach that one buys it back, conclude from it that the incense it mentions among his possessions is non-sacred incense. Evidently its preparation may be in a non-sacred place, and this is difficult for Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “Rav Yehuda teaches,” a reading Rashi rejects.]
gershom:a39.1: Rather, Rav Yosef said: answer it this way: “and there were among them suitable items” is not speaking of the incense itself, but: there was among them one of the ingredients fit for the incense; they are given to the artisans.
gershom:a40.1: 368 maneh: for so comes out the count of the maneh of the eleven ingredients of the incense.
gershom:a41.1: The measure of his full handfuls was close to a peras [half a maneh].
rashi:b1.1: We read: “Once in sixty or seventy years they would blend it by halves”: for they needed to blend only half the measure, because the leftover of sixty or seventy years comes to half the measure of the incense; sometimes at sixty, sometimes at seventy, or close to them, because not all handfuls are equal.
rashi:b2.1: One-third or one-quarter I did not hear: that they would keep the leftover eighty, ninety or a hundred years, so that they needed to blend only a third or a quarter. And an individual who blended a third or a quarter is also exempt.
rashi:b2.2: According to its composition [bematkuntah]: the language of the verse. If he wanted, he would blend the incense each day for its own day; therefore an individual who blended even just one maneh is liable.
rashi:b3.1: The “halves” in Rava’s statement are not precise; rather, any amount fit to be burned.
rashi:b6.1: Crush well, well crush: the appointed official says this to the one grinding.
rashi:b6.2: Speech is detrimental to wine: in tractate Menaḥot, in the chapter Kol HaKorbanot (87a): When the stream of the lees spurted out, the treasurer knocked; for the treasurer knocks with a reed for the one drawing the wine and signals to him without speech, since it is bad for the libations; he would not speak with his mouth, for speech is detrimental to wine.
rashi:b7.1: Eleven ingredients: and above we counted eleven: balm, onycha, galbanum and frankincense; myrrh, cassia, spikenard and saffron, that is eight; costus, cinnamon and aromatic bark, that makes eleven ingredients. They were told to Moses, and only four were specified [in the verse]. Any eleven he wishes he may put in, as long as it is something whose smoke rises, as we expound below through a generalization and a detail, in accordance with Rabbi Yishmael.
rashi:b8.1: But say “spices” is a generalization: that is, from where do we know that the verse comes to count? Perhaps it comes only to be expounded as a generalization and a detail [and a generalization], and not for the count of eleven.
rashi:b8.2: Whose smoke rises [koter]: that rises in a column like a staff and does not branch out here and there.
rashi:b9.1: A type of tree: which is balm [tzori].
rashi:b10.1: It comes for itself: to teach us that even though its smell is foul, we make it part of the incense.
rashi:b10.2: If so: if one needed to expound it only as a generalization and a detail and a generalization, the verse should not have written “spices,” since “Take for you” would imply a generalization. Rather, it put “spices” at the start and also wrote “Take for you,” in order to expound a generalization and a detail and a generalization for “its smoke rises,” as below, and also for the count of eleven.
rashi:b12.1: The school of Rabbi Yishmael: also requires eleven, since it teaches: “Or perhaps,” and so on, and it can be expounded only as he expounds it; and it requires that its smoke rise.
rashi:b13.1: A generalization in the first generalization: the Gemara explains all of it below.
rashi:b15.1: And let them also learn from frankincense, and so on: this is what it challenges with “or perhaps it is only…”: the last detail, that is, frankincense, should also bring what is similar to it, as the first detail does; and the exclusion of something whose scent does [not] diffuse and whose smoke does not rise would then be stated to me, like the other, first details, from which one brings what is similar to them.
rashi:b16.1: If so: if one brings it like the other details, let it write it in the middle, with the other, first details. And that is why it says: No.
rashi:b17.1: And the Gemara challenges it: this is no answer, for had it written frankincense with the other details between the two generalizations, there would be twelve: “spices,” two; stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense, that is six; and “spices” corresponding to them, that is twelve. That is why it did not write it with the detail, so that you should not say twelve are required; but in fact one does learn from it.
rashi:b17.2: If so, let it write it in place of galbanum: so that we would learn from it that there are eleven, and we would learn from it [that one brings an item] even if [its smoke] does not rise; and let it write galbanum at the end. Now, at any rate, we learn nothing from it.
rashi:b18.1: And His bundle: implies that when they are all together, then He has established it on the earth.
rashi:b21.1: To exclude animals: because animals are written in that passage, it could not avoid calling them adam.
rashi:b23.1: Anyone included in applying: anyone who transgresses when he applies it to himself or to others, who is commanded not to apply the anointing oil to a non-priest.
rashi:b23.2: Is included in “it shall not be applied”: others are commanded concerning him not to apply it to him.
rashi:b24.1: To kings and High Priests: after they had been anointed. [Rashi’s heading reads “High Priests.”]
rashi:b25.1: Just as applying is any amount: for we do not find a measure for applying; so too placing is any amount, even though placing in general is an olive-bulk, as is explained below.
rashi:b26.1: Placing in general is an olive-bulk: for we learn it from the placing in “and he shall give to the priest the sacred item,” where eating is written: “And if a man eats a sacred thing” (Leviticus 22:14), and all eating is an olive-bulk.
rashi:b27.1: Initially they were not strangers: for they were anointed at the beginning.
tosafot:b1.1: Once in seventy-two years they would blend by halves [so Tosafot’s heading]: every year they blend three extra maneh, so in seventy-two years that is 216 maneh. Half of 368 maneh is 184; there remain 32 extra maneh. Each year has 365 and a quarter days, so seventy-two years have seventy-two quarter-days, which are eighteen days; remove them from the 32 maneh, since each day one maneh is burned, a peras in the morning and a peras in the evening, and 14 maneh remain. Divide them among the seventy-two years for the High Priest’s full handfuls: his full handfuls come to nearly a fifth of a maneh each year. But at seventy years they could not blend it by halves, for then they would be short six maneh, the extra would be only eight maneh, and it would not suffice for his full handfuls.
tosafot:b3.1: One who blends a peras in the morning: Rabbi [the name is abbreviated] said that this measure, a peras in the morning and a peras in the evening, is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai; if they burned only an olive-bulk in the morning and an olive-bulk in the evening, they have fulfilled the obligation, as is implied in the chapter HaShoḥet.
tosafot:b4.1: Crush well, well crush: so they had it by tradition, that the breath of the voice helps more than silence.
tosafot:b10.1: It is derived from “Take for you”: even though it is a generalization (that is only an explanation) that is not explicit about what it speaks of, and we say in the first chapter of Zevaḥim that one does not expound such a one through a generalization and a detail. However, in a case like this, in the first chapter of Kiddushin, concerning the awl, “and you shall take” is treated as a generalization, even though “and you shall take” is not a generalization but an explanation.
tosafot:b23.1: Anyone included in applying: this is puzzling according to this version: let animals and vessels also be derived from here; then let them be combined and taught together. Why do I need “exempt … exempt” twice?
tosafot:b26.1: For kings and priests, everyone agrees any amount: so that you should not say that just as Rabbi Yehuda deems one liable with an ordinary person [only from an olive-bulk and not] for less than an olive-bulk, so too with anointing for a mitzva; it teaches us that any amount suffices.
gershom:b1.1: Once in seventy-two years [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text]: at the end of every seventy-two years they would blend the incense that year by halves, half the count of maneh we stated. Why so? Because the leftover incense, two and a half maneh [a year] over seventy[-two] years, comes to a count of 180 maneh, and half the incense comes to 184 maneh; and those four maneh that we do not find in the count of the leftovers grow from the small amounts that remained of the peras beyond his full handfuls.
gershom:b2.1: Another version, from the explanation of Rabbi Yitzḥak, of blessed memory: when it teaches “they would blend it by halves,” it does not mean precisely halves, for he would have had to make eight maneh more than half, since the count of the leftovers comes only to 180; for he holds that his full handfuls were exactly a peras. Since it is close to half, it teaches “by halves.”
gershom:b3.1: [A printer’s marker: this belongs to 6b.] Therefore an individual who blended: the incense by halves in order to smell it is liable, for we find blending by halves in the Temple; but blending a third or a quarter, I did not hear that there was such in the Temple.
gershom:b4.1: And the Rabbis say: Every day he would prepare according to its composition: that is, he would not blend that of the whole year together; rather, every day he would prepare what was needed for that day’s measure and bring it in.
gershom:b5.1: “Which you shall make”: he is liable if he made [incense] like it to smell; and it is possible to blend the day’s maneh, a peras in the morning and a peras in the evening.
gershom:b6.1: Twice a year: to renew its scent.
gershom:b7.1: In the summer, scattered: he spreads it out so that it does not grow moldy from the heat.
gershom:b8.1: So that its scent should not dissipate: from the cold.
gershom:b9.1: He says: the treasurer says “Crush well” the whole time he is grinding, because speech is good for the spices at the time of grinding, and speech is bad for wine while it is being drawn off, as we learned in Menaḥot: The stream spurted, he knocked with the reed; that is, to give him a sign to stop it.
gershom:b10.1: And other spices: as written, five, like those above.
gershom:b11.1: And what compels one to learn it this way? It is a strained answer; let them be learned through a generalization and a detail: “But say ‘spices’ is a generalization,” and so on.
gershom:b12.1: An item whose smoke rises: whose smoke rises upward like a column; so too any item whose smoke rises and whose scent diffuses. And from here the others not written among these are included: they are items whose smoke rises, and no others, for there is nothing whose smoke rises except the eleven.
gershom:b13.1: And if you would say, if so: that it comes from a generalization and a detail and a generalization, let it write one detail: stacte.
gershom:b14.1: La’ei: we learn from a generalization and a detail, and all the details are necessary. For had it written stacte, I would say a type of tree, yes, since nataf is a resin that drips from a type of tree, the ketav.
gershom:b15.1: And had it written onycha and not written stacte, I would say, and so on.
gershom:b16.1: And galbanum: why was it necessary? It comes for itself: even though its smell is foul, [it is included] since its smoke rises. And still one can learn from a generalization and a detail.
gershom:b17.1: If so, one can learn from a generalization and a detail: from “Take for you” I derive the first generalization.
gershom:b18.1: For so we find that taking is a generalization, as it is written: “And you shall take,” a generalization; and let it not write “spices.” Rather, conclude from it that “spices” is for the count, as we said.
gershom:b19.1: Another version, from Rabbi Yitzḥak: If so, as you say, that it is a generalization and a detail and galbanum comes for itself, galbanum is derived from “Take for you,” that is, everything needed for the incense. Rather, conclude from it that it is written for the count. And still, how does the count come out? Say the last “spices” are two, like the first “spices,” and not five, and they fall short.
gershom:b20.1: If so: that they are only two, let it write “Take spices spices” together, and at the end write stacte, onycha and galbanum. Rather, since it wrote “spices” at the end, conclude from it as we said. The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: from a generalization and a detail and a generalization.
gershom:b21.1: Or perhaps it is only a generalization in the first generalization, and so on: Rabbi Yishmael wants to learn from both, from the generalization and the detail and from Rav Huna’s count: from the generalization and detail he learns “anything whose smoke rises,” and from the verse he learns how many there are. For if only from the generalization, it is difficult to him: say the last “spices” are two, and so on.
gershom:b22.1: And let it also learn from the last detail, from pure frankincense, that we should bring even those that have only one aspect, like frankincense, whose scent diffuses, and let it take out one of those whose smoke rises, even though [the one brought in its place] does not rise.
gershom:b23.1: He then said: If so, that we learn from it, let the verse write frankincense in the middle, before “spices,” with the other details. Rather, since it wrote it at the end, conclude from it: you cannot learn in accordance with the language, and so on.
gershom:b24.1: If because of this, it is no proof; for had it written frankincense in the middle, there would be twelve, since we would say the last “spices” are six, like the four in the detail and the two in the generalization. Rather, you can say thus: If so, that frankincense comes to be learned from, let it write it in the middle and galbanum at the end, after “spices,” and there would be only eleven. Since it did not write it in the middle, conclude from it that you cannot learn in accordance with the last version, which brings even those with one aspect, but in accordance with the first version, from the generalization and detail: just as the detail is explicit, an item whose smoke rises and whose scent diffuses.
gershom:b25.1: Reish Lakish said: there is no need to learn it either from the count or from the generalization and detail, but from itself, from the name ketoret: what is the meaning of the term ketoret? An item whose smoke rises; and you find none whose smoke rises except these eleven.
gershom:b26.1: [Any fast] that does not include some of the sinners of Israel who repent and fast is not a fast.
gershom:b27.1: From here: “And has established His bundle on the earth”: that is, when they are in one bundle on the earth, the good and the bad, and they break their hearts and return, the Holy One, Blessed be He, has established it: the world endures for their sake.
gershom:b28.1: That one: the “and the people [nefesh adam]” that is written comes to exclude animals; that is, of the people there were sixteen thousand, aside from the animals.
gershom:b29.1: Anyone included in applying: anyone who is warned if he applies it to himself is included in “it shall not be applied”; the other who applied it to him is also liable. And a gentile, since he is not warned if he applies it to himself, is not included in “it shall not be applied”; the other who applied it to him is not liable. Therefore for gentiles too one is exempt.
gershom:b30.1: To kings and to priests: after they had been anointed at their initiation, Rabbi Meir deems him liable and Rabbi Yehoshua [so the text here; the daf reads Rabbi Yehuda] deems him exempt; their reasons are explained below.
gershom:b31.1: And why does Rabbi Yehuda take the measure of an olive-bulk? But Rabbi Yehuda [exempts]! [A printer’s note: it seems it should read “exempts with regard to kings and priests.”] Just as applying, and so on: just as applying is any amount, for with any amount one can apply it to one limb, so too placing, for which there is punishment, is with any amount.
gershom:b32.1: And Rabbi Yehuda holds: we derive placing upon a stranger from placing in general. Just as placing in general is an olive-bulk, as it is written: “And if a man eats a sacred thing in error, then he shall add its fifth to it and give it to the priest,” and that placing (here) [there] is an olive-bulk, which is derived from eating sacred food, for there is no eating with less than an olive-bulk, so too placing upon a stranger is an olive-bulk. But applying to kings and priests not at the time of their initiation, everyone agrees, is with any amount, since there is no placing with them. [A printer’s note: perhaps it should read: “now they are strangers,” and we call them complete strangers.] Initially: at the time of their initiation, and so on, we do not call them complete strangers.
gershom:b33.1: Initially, at the time of their initiation, they are not strangers with regard to the anointing oil.
